linetext: Introductions and procedural discussion
PRESIDENT:  Good morning.  Welcome to all of you.  I hope
you had safe travels.
The members of the tribunal are very happy to meet
with the parties and counsel representatives, we look
forward for this two-week hearing.
We have, before we start the evidentiary hearing
with the opening statements of the respective parties,
I have to review and decide on a few procedural matters.
The first matter on the agenda today is the
participation of Mr Goeth to this hearing and to this
arbitration.
We have received an application from the claimant on
Saturday night and we have received the comments of the
parties.
The second point on the agenda is the use of the
slides and some of the slides identified by parties'
respective counsel as being demonstrative exhibit, this
will be dealt with before we start this morning.
We have these two points on the agenda today before
we start; is there any other point that needs to be
covered before we commence with the evidentiary hearing?

Thank you, there are no other matters at this moment

PRESIDENT:  Thank you, claimant, and very shortly the

the delegation that is composed on my right-hand side.

MR TALANOV:  Thank you, dear members of the panel, a very

being here today.

PRESIDENT:  Thank you.  We will resume in a few minutes.

PRESIDENT:  So we're back on record.

So therefore, the participation of Mr Goeth in this

However, the tribunal is very concerned with the

the hearing commencing today, 16 March 2026.
A procedural order will be issued in the course of

Respondent, you have understood the tribunal is

PRESIDENT:  Thank you.

However, with respect, we must object against this

We believe that the threat to the integrity of these

Again, it is not only about confidentiality.

PRESIDENT:  You just referred to an ICC provision of the

PRESIDENT:  On the waiver, right?
MR HAUGENEDER:  We believe that this is a very serious

PRESIDENT:  Your objection is noted and it's on record.

That being said, each of these slides provides for

So the question here is to the tribunal, the

The tribunal finds that this violation of the

does not -- is not serious enough to exclude those

been submitted in respondent's opening submission.
However, should this happen again, the tribunal puts

and any use of an exhibit, a legal material, in order to
provide a secondary presentation of, in primary, either
exhibit or legal matter through a chart, a form, a flow

exhibit, and the tribunal reserves its right to exclude,
in particular for the examination of the witnesses and
the experts, reserves its right to exclude the use of
the slide for the purpose of cross-examination or
closing submissions.
There are rules in this arbitration and we
appreciate the amount of work put by the parties and the
parties' teams, so that the parties may prepare in
advance for every step of the proceedings.
The preparation of the opening submissions is one of
them and the 72-hour deadline was precisely made in
order to allow the parties not to have to search at the

the slides.
So this is addressed to both parties, but in

respondent.

Should an extension of time be required, we just

Opening submissions by Mr Haugeneder
MR HAUGENEDER:  Madam president, members of the tribunal,
it is a privilege for Ms Petkute, Mr Holland and myself
to present PPD's opening statement in this important
matter.
After introducing some key facts and legal
principles that are highly relevant for the case, we
will first set out PPD's claims for suspended gas
deliveries, then move to PPD's claim on market
manipulation, followed by the quantification of these
claims.
We will then address Gazprom's counterclaims and
conclude with the request for relief.
I move to my introductory points.
First, Gazprom, the respondent in this case, is not
an ordinary corporation, it was one of the most powerful
companies of the world.  Gazprom has the export monopoly
for pipeline gas from the Russian Federation, which
before 2022 was the most important source of gas for
Europe.
So Gazprom had enormous power.
Gazprom is managed by senior political allies of
President Putin.  President Putin has often personally
intervened on matters of Gazprom and has made
representations on behalf of Gazprom.
Gazprom is used as a commercial vehicle for Russian
foreign policy.  It is an instrument of geopolitical
pressure, as you can see from numerous respectable
sources that we have submitted in this arbitration.
The influence of the Russian Government on Gazprom
is also acknowledged by Gazprom itself, as you can see
from these exhibits.
As the European Parliament concluded already before
the events of 2022, Gazprom used its enormous market
power to create dependency relationships throughout
Europe.
These conclusions also apply until 2022 to Croatia.
Croatia required gas imports of around 17 to 24 terawatt
hours since 2017.  The annual contract quantity under
the contract at issue here was 21.1 terawatt hours per
year.
Therefore, the contract delivery volume provided for
most of the gas quantities imported by Croatia.
Through the contractual take or pay obligation
Gazprom had control over a very significant part of
Croatia's gas consumption.
In the month before the full-scale invasion of
Ukraine, Gazprom applied the market power it had built
up with full force and restricted gas supplies in
Europe, creating an artificial scarcity of gas.  Gazprom
disputes this, but the evidence that we have submitted
speaks for itself.
What did Gazprom concretely do?
First, Gazprom cut its sales from the trading
platform ESP, that concerns spot sales, up to full
discontinuation in October 2021.  This means long-term
contracts were generally fulfilled in 2021, but Gazprom
stopped spot sales, creating a very significant deficit
of gas supply.
Second, Gazprom has emptied gas storage in Europe
throughout 2021 and failed to refill them, leaving the
gas storages empty before the winter and causing
additional scarcity during a time of the year when gas
was most needed.
After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the
adoption of wide-ranging sanctions by the European
Union, President Putin directed Gazprom, the Russian
Central Bank and the Russian Government to work out
measures to unilaterally change the currency of payment
of gas supplies for so-called unfriendly countries.
So Gazprom was not just implementing laws and
government regulations; it was instrumental in setting
up an elaborate mechanism to circumvent sanctions.
Decree 172 was issued on 31 March 2022.
The letters which Gazprom sent to European gas
buyer, that requested to change the payment currency to
roubles and to agree on a new payment mechanism, was
sent on 1 April 2022.  This was one day after the
issuance of decree 172.
Clearly, these letters, with which Gazprom
threatened that gas supplies would be interrupted unless
the buyers of gas agree to a changed payment mechanism,
were part of a coordinated action in which Gazprom had
worked in tandem with the Russian State.  These letters
were sent in early afternoon of 1 April, so immediately
after the issuance of decree 172.
That was also freely admitted in the public
statements of Gazprom, such as in the statement of
Mr Miller, the head of PJSC Gazprom, "Our product, our
rules".
Clearly, Gazprom was not a corporation implementing
bona fide regulations.  It was participating in making
these rules.
The mechanism Gazprom imposed on its buyers, and
that you can see here, provided that PPD had to open
a bank account at Gazprombank and instruct Gazprombank
to sell PPD's euros at the Moscow Stock Exchange using
a national clearing centre, the NCC.
However, under this mechanism, PPD would not know
the identity of the buyer of euros with which it
transacted.
The roubles that PPD received from the unknown buyer
of euros would then be transferred to a roubles account
of PPD and from there to Gazprom.
Therefore, the essence of the mechanism was that PPD
would not know with who -- who was buying its euros to
obtain roubles.
I will now move to the consequence of Gazprom's
behaviour for the gas buyers, and there were two main
consequences.
First, the lasting withholding of gas from the
European market caused an unprecedented rise of gas
prices.
The TTF price was stable in 2019/2020 as you can see
here, but spiked in 2021/2022 during the artificial
scarcity of gas.
There is a direct and obvious correlation between
Gazprom's conduct and gas prices up until late 2022,
which you can see from the graph on the right-hand side.
You see the gas supplies going down and the price
spiking.
This was of course immensely profitable to Gazprom
because the cost of production remained largely the
same.
This was not only the case for the contractual TTF
price, but also for other hub prices, like CEEGEX in
Hungary or CEGH in Austria.
There is widespread agreement that the crisis was
caused by Gazprom, that Gazprom manipulated the gas
market despite the record high production at the same
time.
The second consequence of Gazprom's actions in 2022
was the threat to cut off supplies unless buyers
accepted the payment mechanism, which left buyers with
the choice between the interruption of gas supplies
entailing a struggle for survival, or compliance with
the request.
As you can see here, already at the time Commission
President von der Leyen described Gazprom's conduct as
blackmail.
Gazprom indeed cut off supplies to buyers who
refused to comply with the payment mechanism.  The
cut-offs concerned, for instance, Orlen, Bulgargaz
in April 2022, Gasum, GasTerra, Orsted, Shell Energy
in May/June 2022, and ENGIE in August.
Companies highly dependent on Russian gas, such as
OMV or PPD, had no alternative, as you can see here from
OMV's statement, to accepting -- to complying with the
payment mechanism.
The example of Uniper shows that European gas buyers
could not procure gas from alternative sources at
sustainable cost, which in the case of Uniper led to
Uniper's insolvency and forced administration.
Why?  Because the spot market prices were much
higher than those in Gazprom's contract and were
unsustainable for the buyers of Russian gas.
Countries dependent on Russian gas were pushed into
a state of emergency.
In Croatia, an early warning about the emergency
situation on the gas markets was given.  This was the
situation in which PPD had to decide in April 2022
whether to sign Gazprom's terms or face the end of gas
supplies and likely insolvency.
I move now to my third introductory point, the legal
point.  Sanctions imposed by the European Union.
The purpose of sanctions is to increase the cost of
war for Russia.  In broad terms, the sanctions relevant
here prohibited transactions related to the management
of resources or related to assets of the Central Bank of
Russia or of Russian publicly controlled entities, and
they prohibited making available directly or indirectly
funds or economic resources to sanctioned entities.
In addition, there were prohibitions to circumvent
sanctions and to satisfy claims in connection with
transactions effected by sanctions.
In the recently published opinion of Advocate
General Biondi in the Reibel matter, it is once again
confirmed that sanctions are a fundament of European
public policy.
It was also confirmed that sanctions are built on
the principle that they can have significantly negative
consequences for certain economic operators, because
that is their purpose.
The widespread agreement in the authorities is that
EU sanctions must be interpreted broadly to ensure their
effectiveness.
The payment mechanism imposed by Gazprom breached
sanctions in several ways which we set out in detail,
but already from the overview that I have shown, it is
clear that PPD was forced to instruct Gazprombank to
sell euros without knowing the buyer, which obviously
entails the risk, and in fact the high likelihood, that
euros were made available to sanctioned entities,
including the CBR.
The European Commission confirmed this in commenting
on an application of Croatia's High Commercial Court in
the bank guarantee case related to this arbitration as
well as the Croatian Government.
The referral was rejected as procedurally
inadmissible, but that does not change the weight of the
Commission's and the Croatian Government's observations.
It is worth mentioning that in our case, regardless
of the decision on all other issues, sanctions prohibit
any award in favour of Gazprom.
As Advocate General Biondi pointed out in Reibel,
the no claims provision prohibits an award of any claims
if a transaction or its performance has been affected by
sanctions.
So the claim itself need not be covered by other
sanctions provisions, it does not matter whether the
satisfaction of the claims would entail the infringement
of other sanctions provisions, and we submit this is
dispositive of all of Gazprom's counterclaims.
No award can be made in favour of Gazprom.
After having highlighted these points, which we
submit are of fundamental importance for the decision of
the case, I will now give an overview of our legal
submission and its structure.
The legal consequences of the facts of the case are,
first, PPD was not obliged to comply with decree 172 or
decree 254 due to the application of sanctions, due to
article 102 TFEU, PPD did not consent to the variation
of the contract and did not accept to offer -- the offer
to vary the contract.
Even if PPD had consented to the variation, this
consent is invalid because the variation was avoided
with ex tunc effect as it was procured under duress.
Gazprom was not entitled to rely on decree 172 as
a force majeure event.  Gazprom's letter of 1 April
threatening the suspension of deliveries was therefore
an unlawful threat.
PPD has not waived the right to avoid the purported
variation.
Of course, the variations, if they were -- if you
find they were validly agreed, are also invalid due to
the application of sanctions and due to
article 102 TFEU.
Second, as a consequence of the above, PPD was
entitled to pay in euros and refuse payment in roubles.
Third, because PPD had not breached the contract,
Gazprom was not entitled to suspend performance
in November 2022.
Fourth, PPD validly avoided the contract by its
letter dated 8 March 2023.
Gazprom had committed a fundamental breach of
contract by conditioning its contractual obligation to
deliver gas to the modification of the contract in its
favour, and because it refused to accept payment in
euros and suspended gas supplies.
Fifth, as a consequence of Gazprom's breach of
